---

The world has a way of hiding its most interesting parts in plain sight.

On mornings when the light looks ordinary—gray, hesitant, the kind that makes you think the day might be canceled—it’s still doing small work. It slips between curtains. It turns dust into glitter. It makes the edge of a coffee cup look like it belongs to a different, better reality. None of this is dramatic, but somehow it’s always happening. That’s the trick of living: the miracles don’t arrive with trumpets. They arrive with routine.

I used to think that change was a single event, like a door swinging open. A decision. A move. A break. But change is more like weather—an accumulation of tiny shifts you don’t notice until you look back and realize the air has changed. You didn’t become a different person overnight. You just kept walking through days that were quietly teaching you how to stand.

Sometimes I wonder whether memory is an editor. It cuts out the dull parts, smooths the rough edges, and then—decades later—hands you a scene that feels perfectly structured, perfectly lit. But when you actually lived it, it wasn’t like that. It was messy and uneven. It had dead ends and awkward pauses. It was full of thoughts that didn’t go anywhere. Maybe the story you remember is less about what happened and more about what you needed to believe.

There’s a kind of comfort in that. You can’t return to the exact temperature of a moment, the exact tone of someone’s voice, the exact way your hands looked when you held onto hope. But you can still return to the meaning you extracted from it. Meaning is portable. It travels with you.

And then there’s the body—always keeping score in its own language. It remembers without words. It tightens when you’re afraid. It relaxes when you’re safe. It collects tension like dust on furniture, day after day, until one unremarkable breath cracks the surface and you realize you’ve been holding yourself the wrong way for years.

Most days, no one announces that lesson. There isn’t a soundtrack. There’s just a moment—small enough to miss—when you catch yourself, and instead of rushing past, you pause. You feel your feet on the ground. You notice the color of the sky. You let the thought arrive: *Oh. I’m here.*

When you finally notice you’re here, the world doesn’t become perfect. It just becomes available.

That might be the whole point of being alive: not to wait for the dramatic version of happiness, but to practice recognizing what’s real right now. The real might be unglamorous. The real might be a sink full of dishes. The real might be a conversation that goes nowhere. The real might be a quiet room where you sit long enough to stop fighting your own mind.

And even then, something keeps moving forward—like a tide that doesn’t need your approval. You get another chance to choose gentleness. Another chance to make a small repair. Another chance to look up and see that light is still finding its way through the cracks.

So if the day feels ordinary, let it. Ordinary isn’t the opposite of meaningful. Sometimes ordinary is where meaning hides, disguised as routine. You just have to pay attention long enough to recognize it.
